newsitem.title: GREECE: FEATURE - Greek/Turkish Cypriots unite for film.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Greek/Turkish Cypriots unite for film.

text.p: Hailed by some as a revelation and slammed by others as treason, a unique documentary film about the militarily-divided island of Cyprus seeks to help tear down the last remaining wall in Europe.

Made by a Greek Cypriot and a Turkish Cypriot, "Our Wall" traces the island's recent history using heart-rending personal stories from both sides of the barbed wire that has separated their feuding communities since 1974.

"We must face our history and the fact that we have hurt each other. We always speak of our pain but we must also see the other person's pain," said Turkish Cypriot Niyazi Kizilyurek, a political science professor at the University of Cyprus.

Since 1974, when Turkey invaded the island in response to a coup in Nicosia by the military junta then ruling Greece, U.N. peacekeeping troops have kept the Greek Cypriot south and the breakaway Turkish Cypriot north separated.
The film interchanges war footage with bucolic scenes of hospitality and wanderings in deserted old houses and lush green courtyards, images that seem frozen in time in the early 1970s.

A Turkish Cypriot poet remembers her childhood in the south and weeps against a peeling stucco wall while a Greek Cypriot refugee haltingly recounts the murder of her husband and rape of a neighbour by Turkish soldiers.
FILM PROMPTED ACCUSATIONS OF TREASON
The producers said their film has prompted accusations of treason from both sides, especially the Turkish side, which no longer allows Kizilyurek to cross over.

"Niyazi is seen as a traitor who co-operates with the enemy and can no longer see his family in the north," said Greek Cypriot film maker Panicos Chrysanthou. "Some say I too am a traitor and even friends accuse me of giving more time to the Turkish-Cypriot view in the film."
Chrysanthou told Reuters he met Kizilyurek at a conference on the Green Line dividing Cyprus and they both felt their communities could come together again only if they spoke boldy about the past.

"When I met Niyazi in 1988 we discovered we had the same ideas and a great love for Cyprus," he said. "Only if Cyprus is united can we stop fearing for our lives and our future. We must resolve this together, there is no other way."

U.N. efforts to reunite the island in a federation have failed and there has been no peaceful contact between the communities. In the worst violence since the invasion, three Greek Cypriot demonstrators and a Turkish Cypriot soldier have been killed at the Green Line in recent months.

The internationally recognised Greek Cypriot-led government in the south is heavily arming against some 30,000 Turkish troops in the north of the island, described by the United Nations as the most militarised area in the world.

"This may seem Utopian but I believe that if Greece and Turkey spend a fraction of their defence budget so that everyone in both countries sees this film, they would not need arms," said Greek author Nikos Dimou, introducing the film to a Greek audience at Athens Polytechnic University last month.
HISTORY OF HOSTILITIES
The film traces the root of hostilities on Cyprus in the 1950s, when the Mediterranean island was a British colony with a population of 80 percent Greeks and 18 percent Turks.

It shows how a 1955 Greek Cypriot uprising against British rule and the Greek Cypriot quest for Enossis -- union -- with Greece, spread fear in the Turkish minority, which eagerly responded to the colonialists' call to join local police ranks.

Cyprus won its independence in 1960, with Britain, Greece and Turkey as guarantor powers and a constitution giving Turkish Cypriots a vice-president holding power of veto and 30 percent of public sector jobs.

Efforts by Greek Cypriots in 1963 to amend the constitution resulted in bloody clashes between the two communities and the first divisions on the island, with the capital Nicosia crossed by a Green Line and Turkish Cypriots moving to enclaves.
Documentary scenes of the uprooting of Turkish Cypriots in 1964 eerily echoed footage of the Greek Cypriot refugee exodus after the Turkish invasion, 10 years later.
"I didn't know they existed. Nobody told us," said a young Greek Cypriot woman who saw the 1964 Turkish Cypriot refugee camps for the first time in the film.
The 116-minute "Our Wall", which was finished in 1993, has been screened at universities in New York and Athens and private showings in Cyprus.
"We tried to show it to Turkish Cypriots at the Green Line but Turkish authorities stopped them from coming," Kizilyurek said.
Asked to list the main hurdles in re-uniting the island's communities, both men named nationalism, failure to deal with the past and the demographic changes in the north.
"Every time Greek Cypriots demonstrate at the Green Line they drive Turkish Cypriots away," Kizilyurek said.

He said Turkish Cypriots were abandoning the island and being replaced by Turkish settlers from Anatolia -- about 50,000 Turkish Cypriots were now living in London and an estimated 70,000-80,000 settlers have been brought to northern Cyprus.
"Turkish Cypriots have very little power over their fates," he said. "The settlers always vote for the establishment so there is no chance of changing the government, no democracy."
